title: Shopping Cart
description: Cart class with add/remove/setQty/total — the canonical Map-keyed-by-name design that every e-commerce interview problem starts from.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the API surface and the identity rule.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: I need a Cart class supporting add(item, qty), remove(item), setQty(item, qty), and total(). An 'item' is an object with at least a name and a price. I need to handle the case where the same item is added twice — bump the qty, not duplicate the line."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• How are items identified — by name string, by a SKU id, or by object reference? (Almost always name or SKU; reference equality is fragile.)
• If `setQty(item, 0)` — does the row stay with qty 0, or get removed? (Removed is the standard, but worth confirming.)
• Are prices integers (cents) or floats (dollars)? (Floats cause floating-point rounding bugs in totals; cents-as-int is the prod-safe answer.)
• Negative qty — error, no-op, or treat as remove?
sections.why: The identity question — by name vs. by reference — is the single biggest gotcha. If you key the cart by object reference, two `{name: 'apple', price: 1}` literals are different keys, and `add(apple); add(apple)` creates two lines. Asking up-front shows you've seen that bug in real code. The 'setQty(0) removes' question is the API quirk most candidates miss; if you don't handle it, the cart shows phantom zero-qty rows forever. Even framing it as a clarification signals you're thinking about the user-facing consequence.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious array-of-lines design before discarding it.
sections.say:
"The brute force is: an array of `{item, qty}` line objects. `add` does `lines.find(l => l.item.name === item.name)` — if found, bump qty; else push. `remove` does `lines.findIndex(...)` + `splice`. `setQty` is the same find. `total` is `lines.reduce((s, l) => s + l.item.price * l.qty, 0)`.

That works. The problem is the find — it's O(n) per operation, so add/remove/setQty are all O(n). For a five-item cart that's fine; for a thousand-item cart (think bulk B2B order) it stops being fine fast. The fix is to swap the array for a Map keyed by `item.name`. Map.get is O(1), so add/remove/setQty all drop to O(1). Total is still O(n) because we have to visit every line — that's unavoidable."
sections.why: Naming the array version explicitly is what shows you understand the tradeoff. The Map-keyed version reads as 'obvious' only AFTER you've named the O(n)-find problem it solves. Without that framing, an interviewer might think you're just reaching for a Map because Maps feel fancier — and that's a yellow flag. Saying 'array.find is O(n) per op, Map.get is O(1)' is the actual reason, and stating the reason matters more than picking the right structure.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What's the data structure, and what invariants does it enforce?
sections.say:
"The data structure is a Map keyed by `item.name` (or SKU id), with values shaped `{item, qty}`. Two invariants tie the whole API together. (1) Each item.name maps to AT MOST ONE line — `add` of an existing item bumps qty rather than creating a second entry. That's what 'merge duplicates' means in cart-speak. (2) qty is always > 0 in stored lines — `setQty(item, 0)` removes, not zero-out. Otherwise the cart shows phantom rows the user can't get rid of.

Given those invariants, `total` is just a reduce over `lines.values()` — `values()` is critical, not `keys()`, because we need the `{item, qty}` records, not the name strings. The Map's insertion order means iteration is stable, so the line ordering in the cart is whatever order the user added items — usually the desired UX."
sections.why: Naming both invariants is the move. 'Use a Map' alone is a guess; 'Map with two invariants — one-line-per-item, qty>0' is the design. The values()-vs-keys() callout is the load-bearing implementation detail — if you wrote `for (const x of this.lines)` you'd get [name, record] pairs (the default Map iterator), which works but means destructuring twice. Using `.values()` and destructuring `{item, qty}` directly is cleaner and shows you've used Maps enough to know the iterator shapes.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few operation sequences to confirm the model — especially the dedup and setQty(0) cases.
sections.intro: "Let me trace three sequences. Each shows the lines Map (as [name, {price, qty}] pairs) after each op, with the results list collecting every total() output. The first example covers all four operations including the setQty(0)→remove case. The second isolates that quirk. The third checks the empty-cart edge."

examples.input: add 2 apple($1), add 1 bread($3), total, add 1 apple, total, setQty(apple,5), total, remove(bread), total, setQty(apple,0), total
examples.note: Canonical case — exercises every API method. The second `add apple` bumps qty to 3 instead of creating a duplicate line. setQty(apple, 0) removes apple entirely, leaving an empty cart.
Isolates the setQty(0)→remove rule. After setQty(milk, 0) the cart is empty, not 'one milk line with qty 0'. Total reflects empty.

examples.input: total (empty), add 3 egg($1), total, setQty(egg,1), total
examples.note: Empty-cart total is 0 (reduce over empty iterator). setQty replaces the qty rather than incrementing — 3 → 1, not 3 → 4.
examples.trace:
init lines = empty Map
total          → 0 (no lines)     results=[0]
add(egg,3)     → lines={egg:{$1,qty:3}}
total          → 1*3 = 3          results=[0,3]
setQty(egg,1)  → replaces qty 3→1 → lines={egg:{$1,qty:1}}
total          → 1*1 = 1          results=[0,3,1]
return [0,3,1]

sections.why: The first trace catches the dedup bug: if `add` doesn't check for an existing line, the second `add apple` would create a second {apple, qty:1} entry — and Map.set on an existing key would just overwrite to qty:1, dropping the original 2. The merge-into-existing logic is the single line that prevents that. The third example catches the setQty-vs-add confusion: setQty REPLACES the quantity, it doesn't add to it. Candidates who pattern-match 'increment' on every cart op ship this bug routinely.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• add(item) with no qty → default to 1 via the parameter default. Caller should be able to write `cart.add(apple)` and get one of them.
• add an item already in the cart → bump qty, don't duplicate. The trace above demonstrates this.
• setQty(item, 0) → remove, not store-with-zero. The standard cart UX expectation.
• setQty(item, -3) → also remove (qty <= 0 catches both). Don't store negative qty, don't throw.
• setQty for an item NOT in the cart → no-op. The user can't `setQty` something they haven't added — don't auto-insert with a fake price.
• remove for an item not in cart → Map.delete returns false silently, so it's a no-op. Don't throw.
• total() on empty cart → 0 (reduce starts at 0).
• Floating-point prices — `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`. In real prod code, prices live in cents (int) and the display layer formats. In interview scope, the prompt usually uses whole-dollar prices so it doesn't bite.
• Concurrent updates from two browser tabs — out of scope here, but in real code the cart needs server-side reconciliation or last-write-wins."
sections.why: The setQty-on-missing-item case (no-op vs. auto-insert) is the design call most candidates skip past — naming it shows you've thought about API contracts beyond 'works in the happy path'. The floating-point bullet is the production-savvy flag; senior interviewers immediately know you've worked on real e-commerce code if you mention cents-as-int unprompted. It's the kind of edge that doesn't show up in algorithmic prep but absolutely shows up in customer support tickets.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity and place this design?
sections.say:
"Time: add/remove/setQty are O(1) — each is one Map.get plus one Map.set or Map.delete. No iteration. total() is O(n) in the number of unique line items — we have to visit each line to compute price × qty, no shortcut. If we wanted O(1) total, we'd maintain a running subtotal field on every add/setQty/remove — the speedup is real but it adds an invariant (`this.subtotal` must always equal `sum(lines)`) that's easy to get wrong on one of the API methods. I'd start with the O(n) total and only cache if profiling shows it's hot.

Space: O(n) where n is the number of unique line items. The Map's overhead is small; the only thing that grows is the entries themselves.

The 'map keyed by canonical identity' design is the same shape that powers a session store keyed by session-id, a friendslist keyed by user-id, a routing table keyed by URL pattern. Any time you have a collection of records where you need O(1) lookup-by-id AND ordered iteration, Map (not plain Object) is the right tool — Maps preserve insertion order, allow non-string keys, and have a saner API. An LRU cache adds an eviction list on top of this; a versioned-cart adds a change history; the core CRUD-by-key shape stays the same."
sections.why: Naming when to add the subtotal cache (only after profiling) is the senior-engineer move — most candidates either ship it preemptively (and ship the invariant bug) or never mention it. The Map-vs-Object aside is the JS-specific knowledge that separates 'I write JS' from 'I know JS' — Object key coercion (everything becomes a string), no insertion-order guarantee on numeric-looking keys, no .size, are the gotchas that make Object the wrong choice here even though it's syntactically lighter.

walkthrough.intro: Step through a sequence of Cart operations. Each example is an op list — add/remove/setQty/total. The state panel shows the `lines` Map (as [name, {price, qty}] pairs) after each op. The trace collects every total() result into a `results` array so you can verify price × qty math after each change.

examples.label: add 2 apple($1), add bread($3) → total 5; add 1 apple → 6; setQty(apple,5) → 8; remove(bread) → 5; setQty(apple,0) → 0
add 1 milk($2); total → 2; setQty(milk,0) removes → total 0
empty total → 0; add 3 egg($1); total → 3; setQty(egg,1) → 1

trace: const snap = () => [...lines.entries()].map(([k, v]) => [k, { price: v.item.price, qty: v.qty }]);
yield { line: 3, label: 'new Cart() — lines = empty Map', state: { ops, lines: snap(), results: [] } };
const item = { name: o.name, price: o.price };
yield { line: 5, label: 'op#' + k + ': add(' + o.name + ' $' + o.price + ', qty=' + qty + ')', state: { ops, lines: snap(), results: [...results], op: o.op } };
yield { line: 6, label: existing ? 'existing line found: qty=' + existing.qty + ' → bump' : 'no existing line — insert new', state: { ops, lines: snap(), results: [...results], op: o.op } };
yield { line: 7, label: existing.item.name + '.qty += ' + qty + ' → qty=' + existing.qty, state: { ops, lines: snap(), results: [...results], op: o.op } };
yield { line: 8, label: 'lines.set("' + item.name + '", { item, qty: ' + qty + ' })', state: { ops, lines: snap(), results: [...results], op: o.op } };
yield { line: 11, label: 'op#' + k + ': remove(' + o.name + ')', state: { ops, lines: snap(), results: [...results], op: o.op } };
yield { line: 11, label: 'lines.delete("' + o.name + '") → lines=' + JSON.stringify(snap()), state: { ops, lines: snap(), results: [...results], op: o.op } };
yield { line: 12, label: 'op#' + k + ': setQty(' + o.name + ', ' + o.qty + ')', state: { ops, lines: snap(), results: [...results], op: o.op } };
yield { line: 14, label: 'qty<=0 → remove(' + o.name + ') instead of zero-qty row', state: { ops, lines: snap(), results: [...results], op: o.op } };
yield { line: 16, label: o.name + '.qty = ' + o.qty, state: { ops, lines: snap(), results: [...results], op: o.op } };
yield { line: 16, label: 'no line for ' + o.name + ' — no-op', state: { ops, lines: snap(), results: [...results], op: o.op } };
yield { line: 20, label: 'op#' + k + ': total() = ' + (parts.length ? parts.join(' + ') + ' = ' : '') + sum, state: { ops, lines: snap(), results: [...results], op: o.op, sum } };
yield { line: 23, label: 'all ops processed — totals=' + JSON.stringify(results), state: { ops, lines: snap(), results: [...results], returns: JSON.stringify(results) } };

notes: Use a Map keyed by `item.name` (or a SKU id) — array.find is O(n) per add, Map is O(1).
`add` of an existing item must bump qty, not duplicate the line. Easy bug to ship.
`setQty` to 0 should remove the line. Otherwise the cart shows phantom 0-qty rows.

questions.q: Why key the lines Map by `item.name` instead of pushing items into an array?
options: Maps coerce numeric strings to numbers, so SKU-shaped names stay sortable for the line-order view
O(1) lookup on add/remove/setQty instead of O(n) array.find
An array of objects doesn't survive JSON.stringify when objects share property names with array methods
Map.size invalidates on every mutation, forcing recomputation that an array's cached length avoids

questions.q: What should `add(apple)` do when apple is already in the cart?
options: Throw a `DuplicateItemError` — apples are already in the cart and re-adding is a UX mistake
Replace the existing line — the most recent `add` overrides the prior quantity (last-write-wins)
Increment the existing line's qty by the new qty (default 1)
Add a second line for the same item, deduping at checkout instead of at add-time
Throw a RangeError — qty must be a positive integer per the cart contract
Leave a zero-qty line in the cart so the user can still see the item was once chosen
Clamp the value to 1 — carts treat 0 as an underflow and round up to the minimum positive qty
`lines.keys()` returns the Map's internal hash buckets, not the item-name keys you'd expect
values() yields the `{item, qty}` records you need to compute price × qty
`keys()` iterates in hash-bucket order rather than insertion order, breaking the per-line price math
Both work; `values()` is just a stylistic preference because it reads as 'sum the values'

exercises.prompt: Complete Cart.add and total() so adding 2 apples ($1) and 1 bread ($3) totals 5.

L3.prompt: Build a Cart with add/remove/setQty/total. Sequence: add 2 apple ($1), add 1 bread ($3) → 5. add 1 more apple → 6. setQty(apple, 5) → 8. remove(bread) → 5. setQty(apple, 0) → 0.
hints: Store lines in a Map keyed by item.name so add/setQty/remove are O(1).
add must merge into an existing line by bumping qty, not create a duplicate.
setQty(item, 0) should call remove(item) — no phantom zero-qty rows.
